issues.legal_issue: Direct evidence of the acquired land’s own value makes it unnecessary to determine market value from sales of adjacent lands.
material_facts: The claimant had purchased the same 20-acre parcel before its acquisition and admitted that its value had increased tenfold by the time of acquisition.
Applying that admitted increase to the earlier purchase price produced an estimated value for the parcel that corresponded to the Land Acquisition Officer’s award.
The claimant relied on two sale deeds for smaller nearby plots, but the court found that the evidence of the acquired land’s own value was available.
issues.conclusion: The High Court did not err by relying on the evidence of the acquired land’s own value rather than the nearby sale deeds; the Reference Court had erred by overlooking the claimant’s admission.
issues.legal_principle: When evidence of the value of the acquired land itself is available, it is unnecessary to determine value by reference to adjacent lands. The court also relied on State of M.P. v. Santabai and Salgoankar v. Union of India for the principle that the consideration paid by an owner for the land later acquired may form the basis for determining its market value.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns determination of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.owner_purchased_same_land: The owner had purchased the same land that was later acquired.
predicates.owner_admitted_value_change: The owner testified to the change in the land’s value between the purchase and acquisition.

issues.definition: When compensation for acquired land is at issue and the owner’s purchase and testimony provide direct evidence of the land’s value, that value may be determined without relying on adjacent-land sales.

issues.legal_issue: A large acquired parcel should not be valued by applying per-square-foot rates derived from sales of small plots where a prudent purchaser would not buy the large parcel on that basis.
material_facts: The Reference Court used sale deeds for smaller plots to determine compensation on a per-square-foot basis.
The court considered that a willing and prudent purchaser would not buy such a large extent on a per-square-foot basis.
issues.conclusion: The Reference Court committed a manifest error by valuing the large parcel on a per-square-foot basis; the High Court was right to set aside that award.
issues.legal_principle: In assessing market value, the court must consider the position of a willing and prudent hypothetical purchaser and ask whether such a purchaser would buy the land, in the circumstances, on a per-square-foot basis.

issues.definition: When a large acquired parcel is valued using per-square-foot rates from small plots, the parcel should not be valued on that basis if a prudent purchaser would not buy it that way.

issues.legal_issue: Special-leave interference with a High Court’s compensation determination is unwarranted when the High Court applied the correct principle and committed no manifest error of law.
material_facts: The appeal challenged the High Court’s decision setting aside the Reference Court’s enhanced compensation award and confirming the Land Acquisition Officer’s award.
The High Court relied on the claimant’s evidence about the value of the same land and the increase in its value.
The Supreme Court found no manifest error of law or application of a wrong legal principle by the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The case was not fit for interference under Article 136 of the Constitution, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court found no basis to interfere where the High Court had applied the correct principle and had committed no manifest error of law in determining compensation.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_in_compensation_cas: The proceeding is a special-leave appeal challenging a compensation determination.
predicates.high_court_applied_correct_principle: The High Court applied the correct principle in determining compensation.
predicates.record_discloses_no_manifest_error: The record discloses no manifest error of law in the High Court’s determination.

issues.definition: In a special-leave appeal concerning compensation, when the High Court applied the correct principle and the record discloses no manifest legal error, interference is unwarranted.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant who has withdrawn compensation deposited under a Reference Court award must return it when the lower compensation award is confirmed.
material_facts: The claimant had withdrawn money deposited pursuant to the Reference Court’s award.
The Supreme Court confirmed the Land Acquisition Officer’s lower award and held that the respondent was entitled to recover the withdrawn amount.
The Court allowed six months for repayment with the same interest as awarded by the Reference Court.
issues.conclusion: The respondent was entitled to recover the withdrawn amount, with the same interest as awarded by the Reference Court, and the claimant was allowed six months to deposit it.
issues.legal_principle: The judgment applied the consequence of confirming the lower award after the claimant had withdrawn the amount deposited under the higher Reference Court award; it cited no separate statutory provision or earlier case for this repayment direction.
